content_list.content_text: Few movements in cinema have been as influential as the French New Wave, or nouvelle vague. What began as a gathering of ambitious young critics working at a film magazine turned into a group of filmmakers whose work redefined modern cinema.

The movement's origins lie in the strong presence of two individuals: film archivist Henri Langlois and critic André Bazin. The latter was one of the founders, in 1950, of the magazine Cahiers du cinéma; Langlois was a co-founder of the Cinémathèque Française, a film archive that held regular screenings in Paris.

information.contentText: It is considered a cult film and one of the most famous of the French New Wave. It was Jean-Luc Godard's first feature film. The film was shot in less than four weeks. Director Jean-Luc Godard made the film without a finished screenplay, essentially improvising. Godard would write the scenes in the morning so they could be shot later. To make the actors perform more spontaneously, Godard only handed them their lines as the scenes were being shot. "À Bout de Souffle" is a French expression that means, in English, "at the end of one's strength, out of breath", a reference to the character Michel Poiccard's constant flight.

content_list.content_text: Many of the future members of the French New Wave knew Langlois personally and attended the Cinémathèque with almost religious fervor, often discussing the films they had seen into the early hours. Among the filmmakers who later wrote for Cahiers du cinéma were François Truffaut (1932-1984), Jean-Luc Godard (b. 1930), Jacques Rivette (b. 1928), and Eric Rohmer (1920-2010).

The magazine scorned the conservative French cinema of the time and instead championed American directors and the development of an auteur theory. A director's recognizable signature - a personal stamp that defined a filmmaker's work - was seen as a sign of greatness. The Cahiers critics joined other regulars of the Cinémathèque in their desire to make their own films.

content_list.title: Characteristics of French New Wave cinema
content_list.description:
Emphasis on "auteur cinema": this "new wave" brought many innovations. The artists were interested in making auteur-driven cinema, in which the screenplay and the direction were truly valued, as was the acting. It was in this context that the expression "auteur cinema" was coined.
Breaking narrative linearity: One of the elements the French New Wave subverts is linearity. There was no concern with telling the story in the chronological order of events, which led to a rupture in narrative structure.
Emphasis on outdoor settings: Outdoor locations were also widely used. Natural light and everyday settings came to be valued, unlike what had been done until then, when scenes were shot in studios and controlled spaces. The filmmakers wanted to show the pulsing life of the streets, passersby, and everyday life as the backdrop for their stories.
Everyday themes: The themes addressed raised common questions, day-to-day hardships, and mundane reflections on life. Because of this, acting was very important, with improvisation and spontaneity even being emphasized. In addition, other subjects such as romantic and sexual freedom and postwar pacification also appear frequently.
Innovation in filmmaking: On the technical side, the French New Wave experimented with new framings and camera movements, and also innovated in the editing of scenes.

content_list.content_text: Though immature, the early films of Godard, Rivette, and Rohmer marked an aesthetic shift, moving the action from studios to real locations. This was made possible by technological advances, as cheaper high-quality portable cameras and faster film stocks were by then available, allowing access to almost any place and shooting without the aid of lighting.

information.contentText: Le Beau Serge was the first film directed by Claude Chabrol. The director used his hometown as the location and financed the film with an inheritance his wife at the time had received. It is considered the first film of the French New Wave.

content_list.content_text: The French New Wave officially began with Le Beau Serge (1958), directed by Claude Chabrol (1930-2010), but it was Truffaut's The 400 Blows (1959) and Godard's Breathless (1960) that made the biggest waves. After being banned from the Cannes Film Festival in 1958 for his criticism of French cinema, Truffaut triumphed at the festival the following year. Partly autobiographical and shot in the neighborhood where the filmmaker grew up, The 400 Blows stars Jean-Pierre Léaud as Antoine Doinel, a character whose life and loves the director would chronicle in five films over the next 20 years.

At once good-humored, playful, daring, and insolent, Breathless came to be seen as the film that defined the French New Wave. It was based on a story by Truffaut and displayed all the elements that underpinned the movement's style. Godard mixed cinematic and literary references, even going so far as to cast Jean-Pierre Melville (1917-1973) - one of the French directors Cahiers du cinéma admired - as a character in the film.

information.contentText: The film was financed with help from Truffaut's father-in-law, and Truffaut made an almost autobiographical story, inspired by his own experiences between late childhood and early adolescence.

content_list.content_text: According to some sources, it was Melville who suggested that Godard cut the film so that scenes jumped straight into the action, creating the jump cut that disrupted the flow of conventional "invisible" editing. The story itself was disposable, as alluded to by a character in Godard's third film, Vivre sa vie: film en douze tableaux (1962), who says of a book she is reading: "the story is silly, but the book is very well written."

Le Signe du lion (Sign of the Lion, 1962), by Eric Rohmer (1920-2010), was received with less enthusiasm, but its shooting locations and literary references place it in the same group as his colleagues' films. Paris nous appartient (Paris Belongs to Us, 1961), by Jacques Rivette (1928-2016), was the longest of the early New Wave films, but the way it explores Paris makes it one of the most beautiful, even if it lacks the bold sloppiness of Godard's and Truffaut's films.

information.contentTitle: Trailer for Paris Belongs to Us (1961)
information.contentText: In Paris Belongs to Us, Jacques Rivette's camera revels in sweeping shots of the French capital in his debut feature.

content_list.content_text: Claude Chabrol, probably more than any other director of the French New Wave, was always fascinated by a single genre, and he found in it a gold mine for exploring human weakness. After his debut feature, Le Beau Serge, a simple portrait of French provincial life, The Cousins (1959) served as the model for the films that followed it. That same year, À double tour (Web of Passion, 1959) successfully recombined the movement's elements within a more classical narrative. Chabrol kept going down this path, building a distinctive body of work.

Among the films by other directors also considered part of the French New Wave are Cléo from 5 to 7 (1962), which includes a cameo by Godard as a short film within a feature film, and the seductive Happiness (1965), whose portrait of patriarchal society and the silent suffering of a betrayed wife stands in stark contrast to more male-centered films.

quote.quote: Through me, François learned about women, and through him, I learned about cinema.
quote.author: Jeanne Moreau

content_list.content_text: Both were directed by Agnès Varda (b. 1928), whose debut feature, La Pointe Courte (1955), blended a fictional story of an unhappy marriage with documentary scenes of a fishing village caught in an economic crisis. The film was a novelty for its time, both in its narrative structure and in the way it was made, and today it is recognized as a work of contemporary relevance by one of France's greatest filmmakers.

information.contentText: Many critics have cited it as the forerunner of the French New Wave, with historian Georges Sadoul calling it "truly the first film of the nouvelle vague".

content_list.content_text: Alain Resnais (b. 1922) is another director whose early works align with the French New Wave. Last Year at Marienbad (1961) is arguably his most enigmatic film. The screenplay was written by Alain Robbe-Grillet (1922-2008), a member of an avant-garde literary movement - the nouveau roman - whose creative process became intertwined with that of the French New Wave.

Truffaut's Jules and Jim (1962) became one of the emblematic films of the French New Wave. The film, which tells of a love triangle set before, during, and after World War I, uses several techniques and elements that became trademarks of the new style, such as the incorporation of newsreel footage, freeze frames, dolly shots, and voice-over narration.

information.contentTitle: Famous scene from Jules and Jim (1962)
information.contentText: The film stars Jeanne Moreau, who epitomized the actresses of the French New Wave and was described by critic Ginette Vincendeau as "beautiful, but in a natural way, sexy, but at the same time intellectual".

content_list.content_text: It also features a classic score composed by Georges Delerue. In addition, it stars Jeanne Moreau (1928-2017), a symbol of the French New Wave. Moreau also appears in The Lovers (1958), directed by Louis Malle (1932-1995), which proposed an amoral and casual approach to sex - another metaphor present in several works of the French New Wave.

Godard was the most prolific filmmaker of the movement and kept experimenting with genre, showing his love of literature, cinema, and philosophy in films such as A Woman Is a Woman (1961) and Band of Outsiders (1964). Godard's films, like so many others of the French New Wave, are full of references to American cinema - the unscrupulous characters of Breathless and Band of Outsiders (1964) are ardent fans of Hollywood B movies.

quote.quote: Don't use the brakes. Cars are made to go, not to stop!
quote.author: Michel Poiccard (Jean-Paul Belmondo) in Breathless

content_list.content_text: Godard went on to influence generations of younger filmmakers. When Quentin Tarantino (b. 1963) named his production company A Band Apart, he was paying homage to the legendary French director. Pierrot le Fou (1965) would mark the start of the overt politicization of Godard's work, which only grew over the course of the decade.

information.contentTitle: Scene from Last Year at Marienbad (1961)
information.contentText: The film became famous for its enigmatic, unconventional narrative structure, in which reality and fiction blend while temporal and spatial relationships blur. The film's fanciful, dreamlike nature left audiences and critics around the world baffled and fascinated; some praise it as a masterpiece of surrealist-inspired cinema, while others find it simply incomprehensible.

content_list.content_text: Later, the close-knit confrérie of the French New Wave would be torn apart by infighting and quarrels. By the end of the 1960s, Truffaut and Godard were barely speaking. But at the start of the movement, the members of the group generally collaborated and helped one another. The group did not consist only of directors. Among the actors strongly associated with the French New Wave are Jeanne Moreau, Anna Karina, Michel Bouquet, Jean-Paul Belmondo, Jean-Claude Brialy, Stéphane Audran and, of course, Truffaut's cinematic alter ego, Jean-Pierre Léaud. Behind the cameras was another group of frequent collaborators, such as cinematographers Henri Decaë, Sacha Vierny, Nicolas Hayer, Néstor Almendros, and Raoul Coutard, editors Lila Herman, Cécile Decugis, Claudine Bouché, and Agnès Guillemot, and composers Georges Delerue and Michel Legrand.

movies.title: Breathless
movies.overview: A young car thief kills a policeman and tries to persuade a girl to hide in Italy with him.

movies.title: Jules and Jim
movies.overview: In the carefree days before World War I, introverted Austrian author Jules strikes up a friendship with the exuberant Frenchman Jim. Both men fall for the impulsive and beautiful Catherine, but it's Jules who wins her hand. After the war, Jim visits Jules, Catherine and their daughter in their Austrian home and discovers not only that his feelings for Catherine are unchanged, but also that they're reciprocated.

movies.title: The 400 Blows
movies.overview: For young Parisian boy Antoine Doinel, life is one difficult situation after another. Surrounded by inconsiderate adults, including his neglectful parents, Antoine spends his days with his best friend, Rene, trying to plan for a better life. When one of their schemes goes awry, Antoine ends up in trouble with the law, leading to even more conflicts with unsympathetic authority figures.

movies.title: Cléo from 5 to 7
movies.overview: Agnès Varda eloquently captures Paris in the sixties with this real-time portrait of a singer set adrift in the city as she awaits test results of a biopsy. A chronicle of the minutes of one woman’s life, Cléo from 5 to 7 is a spirited mix of vivid vérité and melodrama, featuring a score by Michel Legrand and cameos by Jean-Luc Godard and Anna Karina.

movies.title: Hiroshima Mon Amour
movies.overview: The deep conversation between a Japanese architect and a French actress forms the basis of this celebrated French film, considered one of the vanguard productions of the French New Wave. Set in Hiroshima after the end of World War II, the couple -- lovers turned friends -- recount, over many hours, previous romances and life experiences. The two intertwine their stories about the past with pondering the devastation wrought by the atomic bomb dropped on the city.

movies.title: Le Beau Serge
movies.overview: François returns to his village after a long absence. He finds his friend Serge who has married Yvonne, and has developed an alcohol problem after the death of their stillborn child. Serge has become an angry, bitter figure not unlike the roles of James Dean, refusing to face reality and adulthood and François must help him.

movies.title: Vivre Sa Vie
movies.original_title: Vivre sa vie: film en douze tableaux
movies.overview: Twelve episodic tales in the life of a Parisian woman and her slow descent into prostitution.

movies.title: Band of Outsiders
movies.overview: Cinephile slackers Franz and Arthur spend their days mimicking the antiheroes of Hollywood noirs and Westerns while pursuing the lovely Odile. The misfit trio upends convention at every turn, be it through choreographed dances in cafés or frolicsome romps through the Louvre. Eventually, their romantic view of outlaws pushes them to plan their own heist, but their inexperience may send them out in a blaze of glory -- which could be just what they want.

movies.title: The Lovers
movies.overview: A shallow, provincial wife finds her relationship with her preoccupied husband strained by romantic notions of love, leading her further towards Paris and the country wilderness.

content_list.subtitle: The events that shaped the world
content_list.title: Timeline of Events from 1940 to 1959
content_list.description: Asian cinema gains even more prominence with the release of several masterpieces. Film noir emerges and musicals continue to shine on the big screen. The Western holds on to its reign as one of the most popular genres, and one of the most important movements in cinema takes place in France: the French New Wave.
